newsitem.title: UK: CRICKET-ENGLAND ENDURE MISERABLE RECORD AT WORLD HEADQUARTERS.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-ENGLAND ENDURE MISERABLE RECORD AT WORLD HEADQUARTERS.

text.p: Wars have raged, governments tumbled and empires disintegrated since England last beat Australia at world cricket's headquarters.
Lord's, venue of the second Ashes test starting on Thursday, has traditionally brought out the best in Australia and the worst in England since the home side won by an innings in 1884.
England's only victory this century came 50 years later, when Yorkshire left-armer Hedley Verity exploited an old-fashioned sticky wicket to bowl his side to an innings' win.
Verity, later to die in an Italian prisoner-of-war camp, took 14 wickets in a day and 15 for 104 overall as England romped to victory by an innings and 38 runs.
Since those distant days the Lord's test, staged at the height of the English summer sports season, has inspired Australia and seemingly intimidated England.
In 1938, Walter Hammond, at his imperious best, drove majestically to score 240 out of an England total of 494. Bill Brown responded with an unbeaten 206 and the match was drawn.
Brown returned 10 years later with Don Bradman's wonderful 1948 side, still regarded as the best side to tour the old country.

This time he could not command a regular test spot in a batting lineup headed by Arthur Morris and Sid Barnes, followed by Bradman, Keith Miller, Lindsay Hassett and eventually the precocious Neil Harvey.
Australia made no contest of the Lord's test with Morris and Barnes both scoring centuries and Ray Lindwall, a Rolls Royce among fast bowlers, taking eight wickets in the match.

Lindwall was back in 1953 in a team captained by Hassett, this time taking seven wickets. Miller, his partner in crime with the new ball who customarily reserved his best for Lord's, scored 109 in the second innings.
Australia were denied victory when Willie Watson played his finest innings for England with 109 while Trevor Bailey, who defied Australia throughout the series with both bat and ball, scored 79.
Miller, the most glamorous figure ever to step on to a cricket field and a member of a generation who never confused sport with war, ensured Australia's sole victory of the 1956 series.
In a low-scoring match, Miller scored 28 and 30 while taking five wickets in each innings.
Troubled by a knee injury which hastened his retirement and without Lindwall who missed the match through injury, Miller gave a masterly exhibition of swing and seam.
Richie Benaud at last turned promise into performance with a dashing 97, as well as taking a sensational catch at gully off a square drive from Colin Cowdrey.
By 1961, Benaud was the Australian captain, fresh from a riveting series with Frank Worrell's 1960 West Indians and promising similar excitement in England.
Injury kept Benaud out of the Lord's test, with Harvey leading his country for the first and only time in his career.

On a pitch giving maximum assistance to the pace bowlers, Alan Davidson took five wickets in England's first innings and Graham McKenzie started an illustrious career with five for 37 in the second. Bill Lawry's 130 in Australia's first innings the only century of the match, proved the difference as Australia won by five wickets.

Rain ensured draws in 1964 and 1968 while in 1972 Bob Massie, swinging the ball at will, made the most impressive debut in Ashes history with 16 wickets in an eight-wicket victory for Australia. Greg Chappell was at his elegant best with a century for the tourists.

Tony Greig led from the front in 1975 in his first match as England captain with 96, David Steele defied Dennis Lillee and Jeff Thomson with 50 while John Edrich scored 175 in the second innings in a drawn match. Australia's Ross Edwards was out one short of a century in the tourists' first innings.
Australia had the better of the drawn test in 1977 and again in 1981, Ian Botham's last test as England captain.
Botham made a pair and walked back to a silent pavilion. Within weeks, under Mike Brearley, he had won the series practically single-handed.
Captain Alan Border hit 196 in Australia's only win of the 1985 series, the start of a hat-trick of victories.

Four years later, with England in increasing disarray, Steve Waugh added an unbeaten 152 to his first test 177 not out while Terry Alderman bemused the England batsmen with five wickets in each innings.

In 1993, Border celebrated his final test at Lord's with a crushing innings victory, courtesy of first innings centuries from Mark Taylor, Michael Slater and David Boon. Shane Warne compounded England's misery with four wickets in each innings.

Taylor, who saved his place with a century in the first test, leads his country at Lord's this week for the first time. Unexpectedly one down in the six-test series, he will hope history at least is again on the Australian side.
